text.div: Aortic regurgitation, managed medically or surgically

Dear colleague, I am writing to inform you about the recent admission of your 89-year-old male patient, who presented with symptomatic aortic valve regurgitation. On admission, he reported progressive dyspnoea and reduced exercise tolerance. Clinical examination confirmed signs of volume overload. Transthoracic echocardiography demonstrated significant aortic regurgitation with preserved left ventricular function. A chest X-ray and ECG were performed, complementing the workup. Blood tests revealed mildly elevated natriuretic peptides without significant renal impairment. Given the patient's advanced age and comorbidities, the multidisciplinary team concluded that surgical intervention carried prohibitive risk. Medical management was optimised with vasodilator therapy and diuretics. The patient responded favourably, with symptomatic improvement prior to discharge. He has been counselled regarding activity limitations and medication adherence. Please continue monitoring fluid status and blood pressure closely in the outpatient setting. We remain available for further consultation.
